title: Response ISO 27001 Awareness Game
description: Multiple-choice scenario game about information security at Response B.V., based on the ISMS (handbooks, employee information security policy, incident register).

categories.title: Phishing & Social Engineering
categories.intro: Recognize suspicious emails, phone calls, and requests before they cause damage.

questions.scenario: You receive an email that appears to be from the director: an urgent request to make a payment quickly, outside the normal procedure.

options.text: Do it right away, it's the director after all
options.feedback: This is exactly what CEO fraud looks like: urgent, unusual, and outside the normal procedure.

options.text: Verify the request through another channel (by phone) before doing anything, and report it
options.feedback: Exactly right. Always verify unusual requests through another channel, and report suspicious attempts.

options.text: Ignore it and do nothing further
options.feedback: Close, but not quite: not acting on it is right, but you should also report it so others can be warned.

options.text: Forward it to colleagues to ask what they think
options.feedback: This delays things and spreads the risk. Verify through an official channel and report it.

questions.explanation: Impersonation, including phishing and CEO fraud, is explicitly listed in the threat catalogue. Always verify unusual requests through another channel and report suspicious emails immediately.

questions.scenario: You accidentally click a link in a suspicious email before realizing it was phishing.

options.text: Say nothing, probably nothing bad happened
options.feedback: Especially when in doubt: report it. Not reporting is the mistake, not the slip-up itself.

options.text: Report it immediately through the internal reporting process, even if it feels uncomfortable
options.feedback: Correct. 'Mistakes are allowed, not reporting them isn't' exists for exactly this situation.

options.text: Try to fix it yourself by restarting the computer
options.feedback: A restart doesn't undo a possible infection and delays the report.

options.text: Wait until you're sure something is actually wrong
options.feedback: Don't wait for certainty — report it right away, even if you're unsure.

questions.explanation: The policy is explicit: report security incidents immediately through the internal reporting process. 'Mistakes are allowed, not reporting them isn't.'

questions.scenario: A stranger calls claiming to be IT support and asks you to confirm your password 'for a check'.

options.text: Give the password, IT support probably needs it
options.feedback: IT support never needs your password. This is a classic social engineering trick.

options.text: Never share passwords, not even with (supposed) IT support, and report it as a suspicious attempt
options.feedback: Correct. Passwords are never shared, least of all over the phone.

options.text: Give a different (fake) password to test them
options.feedback: This still gives the attacker information and signals that you're cooperating. Don't do it.

options.text: Hang up and do nothing further
options.feedback: Hanging up is fine, but still report the attempt so colleagues can be warned.

questions.explanation: Passwords and accounts are never shared — with anyone, through any channel. Suspicious requests for them are reported.

questions.scenario: You recognize a phishing email that was sent to a colleague.

options.text: Warn your colleague right away and report it through the internal reporting process
options.feedback: Good catch. Information security is everyone's responsibility.

options.text: Do nothing, it's not your responsibility
options.feedback: Every employee is responsible for the security of information and systems.

options.text: Reply to the email yourself to unmask the sender
options.feedback: Replying can confirm to the attacker that the address is active. Don't — report it instead.

options.text: Delete the email from your colleague's inbox without saying anything
options.feedback: Without a report, the risk stays invisible to the organization. Always report it.

questions.explanation: A positive reporting culture means everyone takes responsibility, including for risks that affect a colleague.

categories.title: Passwords & Access
categories.intro: Strong passwords, MFA, and never sharing access.

questions.scenario: You need to come up with a new password for a work account.

options.text: A short password that's easy to remember
options.feedback: Short, memorable passwords are exactly the risk this policy aims to prevent.

options.text: A passphrase generated by Bitwarden
options.feedback: Correct. Password management runs exclusively through Bitwarden Business.

options.text: The same password as your personal email
options.feedback: Reusing passwords is a known weakness — never use the same password in multiple places.

options.text: Write the password on a note next to your screen
options.feedback: A visible note makes the password accessible to anyone in the room.

questions.explanation: Password management runs exclusively through Bitwarden Business; a strong, unique password plus MFA is required.

questions.scenario: A colleague asks if he can temporarily log in with your account because his own is blocked.

options.text: Sure, just this once won't hurt
options.feedback: Sharing accounts is never allowed, not even 'just once'.

options.text: No — accounts are never shared; refer him to HR/Security Manager for recovery through identity verification
options.feedback: Correct. Recovering a blocked account goes through HR/Security Manager, not a borrowed account.

options.text: Write down your password and give it to him
options.feedback: Writing it down and handing it over is still sharing a password — not allowed.

options.text: Log in for him yourself and take over his work
options.feedback: This bypasses access management and the need-to-know assignment of rights.

questions.explanation: Access follows need-to-know per person. Accounts and passwords are never shared; recovery goes through HR/Security Manager.

questions.scenario: Your account gets locked after 5 failed login attempts, in the middle of the workday.

options.text: Reset it yourself through a link you were sent
options.feedback: Recovery goes through a verified, formal process, not a random link.

options.text: Just wait, it'll sort itself out by tomorrow
options.feedback: During the day the lockout is 10 minutes or requires verification — waiting until tomorrow isn't needed, and it won't resolve automatically outside working hours.

options.text: Contact HR/Security Manager for identity verification
options.feedback: Correct. Recovery after a lockout goes through HR/Security Manager identity verification.

options.text: Have a new account created
options.feedback: A new account bypasses the recovery process and leaves the old account blocked and unmanaged.

questions.explanation: Lockout after 5 failed attempts (10 minutes during the day, permanent outside working hours); recovery goes through HR/Security Manager identity verification.

questions.scenario: You step away from your desk for a cup of coffee.

options.text: Leave the laptop open, you'll be right back
options.feedback: Even 'a moment' is enough time for someone to look over your shoulder or take action.

options.text: Lock the laptop/screen before walking away
options.feedback: Correct. Devices are always locked when unattended, no matter how briefly.

options.text: Just dim the screen
options.feedback: Dimming doesn't lock anything — the session stays accessible.

options.text: Only lock it if you'll be away for more than 10 minutes
options.feedback: There's no minimum time: lock it every time you step away.

questions.explanation: Laptops and phones are locked every time they're unattended, regardless of duration.

categories.title: Clean Desk & Clear Screen
categories.intro: Desks, printouts, and whiteboards that no one else should see.

questions.scenario: You're heading home. A printout with customer data is still on your desk.

options.text: Leave it, you'll tidy up tomorrow
options.feedback: Confidential information would then sit unmanaged overnight.

options.text: Store it in a locked drawer/cabinet, or shred it right away
options.feedback: Correct. This is exactly the clean desk principle in practice.

options.text: Toss it in the regular bin
options.feedback: A regular bin doesn't protect confidential information — use the shredder.

options.text: Take it home to read at leisure
options.feedback: Company information shouldn't leave the building uncontrolled.

questions.explanation: Paper with confidential information is destroyed via a cross-cut shredder or stored securely — never left unattended.

questions.scenario: You're working on a confidential document while on the move (train, café).

options.text: Just keep working, no one's really watching
options.feedback: Shoulder surfing is a real risk in public spaces.

options.text: Shield your screen or postpone the work until you're in a secure setting
options.feedback: Correct. Working remotely follows the same clean desk/clear screen principle as the office.

options.text: Type extra fast so no one can read it
options.feedback: This doesn't protect the screen from being seen.

options.text: Turn the screen toward the window
options.feedback: That makes it more visible to people outside, not less.

questions.explanation: Remote work follows the same principles as the office: a private space or a shielded screen when working with confidential material.

questions.scenario: An unescorted visitor is walking around the office.

options.text: Not your problem, reception will handle it
options.feedback: Unauthorized access to the building is a recognized risk everyone should stay alert to.

options.text: Approach and escort them, or report it to the right person
options.feedback: Correct. Unescorted visitors are actively approached or reported.

options.text: Ignore it as long as they don't touch anything
options.feedback: Even without physical contact, an unescorted visitor can look or listen in.

options.text: Ask for ID and then let them continue on their own
options.feedback: ID alone isn't enough — escorting is still needed.

questions.explanation: Uncontrolled access by outsiders to the building or network is listed as an explicit threat — actively intervening is the norm.

questions.scenario: You leave a meeting room where the whiteboard is still full of confidential information.

options.text: Leave it, the next group will probably wipe it
options.feedback: You can't guarantee who uses the room next or what they'll do with it.

options.text: Wipe it yourself, or take a photo for your own notes and delete it securely afterward
options.feedback: Correct. Confidential information shouldn't stay visible for the next people using the room.

options.text: Take a photo and share it in the team chat as meeting notes
options.feedback: Sharing an uncontrolled photo of a whiteboard can spread sensitive information widely.

options.text: Lock the door and leave the whiteboard as is
options.feedback: A locked door doesn't actually protect the information itself.

questions.explanation: Company information is only shared with authorized people — leaving it visible for the next room users unintentionally goes against that.

categories.title: Data Sharing & Cloud
categories.intro: Where information may and may not go.

questions.scenario: You need to share a large file with a customer.

options.text: Via WeTransfer, it's fast and free
options.feedback: WeTransfer is explicitly on the list of non-approved cloud services.

options.text: Via OneDrive or Teams, the approved company storage
options.feedback: Correct. Only OneDrive/Teams are approved for sharing files.

options.text: Via your personal Google Drive
options.feedback: Personal cloud services fall outside the organization's management and encryption.

options.text: Via your personal Dropbox account
options.feedback: Dropbox is also on the list of forbidden, non-approved cloud services.

questions.explanation: Uploads to non-approved cloud services such as Dropbox, Google Drive, and WeTransfer are forbidden — only OneDrive/Teams are approved.

questions.scenario: You need to share a password or API key with a colleague.

options.text: By email
options.feedback: Email is not the designated channel for sharing secrets.

options.text: Via the internal team chat
options.feedback: Chat messages aren't meant for sharing confidential credentials.

options.text: Via the internal secrets portal (encrypted, Bitwarden)
options.feedback: Correct. Secrets are only shared in encrypted form, via the internal secrets portal.

options.text: Tell them out loud and have them memorize it
options.feedback: This isn't traceable and isn't practical for complex, generated passwords.

questions.explanation: Confidential information such as passwords, secrets, and certificates is only sent in encrypted form, via the internal secrets portal.

questions.scenario: You want tests to run faster by using production data in the development environment.

options.text: Just do it, it stays internal anyway
options.feedback: 'Internal' isn't the same as allowed — production data is explicitly forbidden in test/development environments.

options.text: Only use fictional or generated test data
options.feedback: Correct. Test and development environments use exclusively fictional or generated data.

options.text: Copy production data and delete it right after the test
options.feedback: Even temporary use of production data in a test environment isn't allowed.

options.text: Just ask a colleague if it's fine
options.feedback: This is a policy rule, not an individual judgment call between colleagues.

questions.explanation: Test and development environments use exclusively fictional or generated data; production data is forbidden there.

questions.scenario: Microsoft Purview (DLP) warns that your email might contain a national ID number.

options.text: Ignore the warning and send it anyway
options.feedback: The warning exists precisely to prevent sensitive data from leaving uncontrolled.

options.text: Check whether it's accurate and remove or secure the sensitive data before sending
options.feedback: Correct. The DLP warning is meant to make you stop and check.

options.text: Paste the text into another program to bypass the check
options.feedback: Deliberately bypassing a security control is itself a violation.

options.text: Rename the file so it isn't recognized
options.feedback: This is also an attempt to bypass the control rather than solve the problem.

questions.explanation: Microsoft Purview flags sensitive data such as national ID numbers, bank account numbers, and personal data to prevent or review sending it — not to be bypassed.

categories.title: Remote Work & Mobile Devices
categories.intro: Working safely outside the office and with mobile devices.

questions.scenario: You're working from home today and need to log in to internal systems.

options.text: Just use your home wifi, no extra steps
options.feedback: Remote work always requires a secure connection, no matter how trusted your home network feels.

options.text: Via VPN with MFA
options.feedback: Correct. VPN and MFA are required when working remotely.

options.text: Via a nearby public hotspot
options.feedback: Public hotspots have unpredictable security — don't use them for company access.

options.text: Via a personal laptop that's a bit faster
options.feedback: Only company-approved devices may be used to access company systems.

questions.explanation: Working from home requires VPN and MFA, along with endpoint security on a company-approved device.

questions.scenario: Your company laptop is stolen from your car.

options.text: Buy a new one yourself and report it later
options.feedback: Loss or theft must be reported immediately, not delayed.

options.text: Report it immediately through the internal reporting process
options.feedback: Correct. Loss or theft of equipment is always reported immediately.

options.text: Wait until you're sure it won't turn up
options.feedback: Don't wait — report it right away, regardless of the chance it's recovered.

options.text: Just let your manager know informally
options.feedback: This must go through the official reporting process, not just an informal heads-up.

questions.explanation: Loss of mobile equipment is a recognized threat; reporting it immediately through the internal reporting process is required.

questions.scenario: You want to quickly put a company file on your personal laptop to keep working on it tonight.

options.text: Fine, it's for work after all
options.feedback: The purpose of the file doesn't make it allowed — the device needs to be company-approved.

options.text: Don't: company files belong only on company-approved devices
options.feedback: Correct. Personal devices fall outside the organization's management and security.

options.text: Okay, as long as you delete the file afterward
options.feedback: Even temporary use on a personal device isn't allowed.

options.text: Okay, as long as it's sent by email
options.feedback: The delivery channel doesn't change the fact that the device isn't approved.

questions.explanation: Company files belong exclusively on company-approved devices and secure storage, never on personal devices or drives.

questions.scenario: You want to use a USB stick to transfer files.

options.text: Any USB stick works fine
options.feedback: USB ports are blocked by default — a random stick won't simply work.

options.text: USB ports are blocked by default; only use approved, encrypted media
options.feedback: Correct. Only encrypted, approved media are allowed, and even then under policy.

options.text: Only use it if the stick is small enough not to be noticed
options.feedback: The size of the stick has nothing to do with whether it's allowed.

options.text: Fine, as long as it's your own personal stick
options.feedback: Personal, unmanaged media are exactly the risk this policy aims to prevent.

questions.explanation: USB ports are blocked by default via Intune; use of media is only allowed with encryption and under the applicable security policy.

categories.title: Reporting Incidents
categories.intro: What to do the moment something goes wrong or looks suspicious.

questions.scenario: You notice a system behaving strangely and suspect malware.

options.text: Try to fix it yourself before reporting anything
options.feedback: Acting on your own can erase evidence or make the problem worse.

options.text: Report it immediately and have the system isolated, don't fix it yourself
options.feedback: Correct. The principle is: report immediately, don't act on your own.

options.text: Turn the system off and leave it at that
options.feedback: Turning it off without reporting leaves the problem unnoticed and unresolved.

options.text: Wait and see if the problem goes away on its own
options.feedback: Waiting increases the risk of further damage or spread.

questions.explanation: The response process is: isolate → scan → report → remediate → evaluate. The principle is to report immediately, not act on your own.

questions.scenario: You suspect personal data is involved in an incident.

options.text: That doesn't need to be reported separately, the incident process already covers it
options.feedback: Personal data requires a separate, fast route via the Privacy Officer.

options.text: The Privacy Officer is informed immediately; a report to the data protection authority may follow within 72 hours
options.feedback: Correct. This is exactly the legal data breach procedure.

options.text: Wait until the next regular meeting
options.feedback: The 72-hour deadline for the data protection authority leaves no room to wait for a regular meeting.

options.text: Decide for yourself whether it's a data breach and do nothing further
options.feedback: This assessment belongs to the Security Officer and Privacy Officer together, not an individual judgment.

questions.explanation: When personal data is involved, the Privacy Officer is informed immediately; a data breach must be reported to the data protection authority within 72 hours (GDPR Art. 33).

questions.scenario: Where do you report an information security incident?

options.text: Through an informal message to a colleague
options.feedback: An informal message isn't logged centrally or followed up.

options.text: Through the incident form in Zammad
options.feedback: Correct. This is the official reporting channel, followed up by the Security Officer.

options.text: Verbally during the coffee break
options.feedback: This isn't recorded and can easily be forgotten.

options.text: In a personal note to yourself
options.feedback: A personal note doesn't reach anyone who can act on it.

questions.explanation: Reports go through the incident form in Zammad; serious reports go directly to the Security Officer or management.

questions.scenario: How quickly can you expect feedback after reporting an incident?

options.text: Never, reports usually disappear into the system
options.feedback: Feedback is a fixed part of the process.

options.text: Within 5 working days
options.feedback: Correct. Feedback within 5 working days is the standard.

options.text: Within a year, during the annual review
options.feedback: That's far too late for an individual report.

options.text: Only if you actively ask for it yourself
options.feedback: Feedback is given proactively, not only on request.

questions.explanation: Every report is followed by feedback within 5 working days, as part of the positive reporting culture.

categories.title: Social Media & Work/Personal Boundaries
categories.intro: Where the line is between work and personal life online.

questions.scenario: You want to post something on LinkedIn about an interesting project at Response.

options.text: Just post it, the project is almost finished anyway
options.feedback: The project's status doesn't change the confidentiality of the details.

options.text: Be careful and don't share confidential company information
options.feedback: Correct. Being careful and not sharing confidential information comes first.

options.text: Add customer names for extra credibility
options.feedback: Sharing customer information without consent is a breach of confidentiality.

options.text: Add a screenshot of an internal system
options.feedback: Screenshots of internal systems can unintentionally reveal sensitive information.

questions.explanation: Care is required on social media and other outlets; sharing confidential company information is forbidden.

questions.scenario: You also use your work phone for personal email.

options.text: Fine, everyone does that
options.feedback: It's explicitly not allowed, no matter how common it feels.

options.text: Not allowed: no personal email on company equipment
options.feedback: Correct. Work and personal use of equipment are kept separate.

options.text: Only outside working hours
options.feedback: The time of day makes no difference — it's about the device, not when you use it.

options.text: Only if you use a separate app
options.feedback: A separate app doesn't change the fact that it's company equipment.

questions.explanation: Personal email on company equipment is not allowed — work and personal stay separate.

questions.scenario: You receive a work-related request containing confidential information on your personal phone.

options.text: Just reply from your personal app
options.feedback: Confidential work communication shouldn't run through personal channels.

options.text: Keep work and personal communication strictly separate and reply through company means
options.feedback: Correct. This is exactly why work and personal communication stay strictly separate.

options.text: Forward the message to friends to ask their opinion
options.feedback: This spreads confidential information outside the organization.

options.text: Ignore it, it's your personal time
options.feedback: Ignoring it doesn't resolve the underlying risk — respond through the right, separate channel.

questions.explanation: Work and personal communication are kept strictly separate, even when a request arrives on a personal channel.

questions.scenario: You lose your smartphone, which also contains business apps.

options.text: Only call your provider to block the SIM card
options.feedback: This protects the SIM card, but not the business data and apps on the device.

options.text: Report it immediately, so the device can be remotely locked or wiped
options.feedback: Correct. Reporting it immediately enables managed remote action.

options.text: Wait and see if someone returns it
options.feedback: Waiting increases the risk that sensitive data remains accessible in the meantime.

options.text: Just buy a new phone and move on
options.feedback: Without a report, the lost device with business access remains an open risk.

questions.explanation: Mobile devices are centrally managed; reporting loss or theft immediately makes it possible to remotely lock or wipe the device.
